evidence_establishes: No prior work was retrieved for this exact question; thus nothing is established or falsified from historical records.
evidence_does_not_establish: Historical evidence is absent, so it does not establish testability, effect sizes, or potential pitfalls for this specific question.
own_inferences: The question is testable in principle with the available data, assuming reliable role definitions are available from independent sources or prior seasons.
Lineup coverage (presence of at least one organizer, shaper, terminal) is a possession-level binary that can be computed from play-by-play and substitution data.

Within-team variation in coverage is likely to exist mechanically unless all of a team's lineups include all three roles; the nontrivial aspect is whether this variation persists after controlling for player availability and talent.
Separability from talent/counts can be examined by regressing coverage on team-level talent metrics and testing for remaining variance.
Talent control behaviour likely refers to checking that the coverage–outcome relationship remains stable when talent is included as a covariate, a test of robust inference.
Even with 420k possessions, statistical power for interaction or within-team variance tests may be limited if coverage is rare.
uncertainties: The exact method for defining organizer, shaper, terminal roles is not specified; if derived from the same play-type data used for analysis, circularity and lookahead bias could invalidate tests.
It is unclear whether roles are player-level (stable across the season) or possession-level (which would require real-time identification and risk measurement error).
The outcome variable that talent control should stabilise is unstated; the question may be incomplete without a specific outcome of interest.
Confounding from coaching decisions, game state, and injuries may be severe, and traditional controls may not fully address endogeneity.
Within-team variance in coverage may be so small in some teams that it is indistinguishable from noise, reducing power.

historical_effect.explanation: No prior work was retrieved, so the decision is based entirely on the current methodological assessment of the question and data.

blocking_constraints.text: The reliability and validity of role assignments (organizer, shaper, terminal) are critical. If roles are not defined a priori with high inter-rater or out-of-sample consistency, the exposure variable is noisy and tests will fail.
If most teams have coverage in >95% or <5% of possessions, within-team variation is virtually absent, making variance-based tests uninformative.
Lineup selection is endogenous (coach decisions, injuries, matchups) and may create spurious correlations between coverage and outcomes that are not separable from talent.
If role definitions are built from the same game events that are used to measure coverage and outcomes, temporal leakage artificially inflates associations.

prior_work.summary: No earlier studies from this project were found that directly address lineup coverage defined by organizer, shaper, terminal roles or its separability from talent.

risks.text: Roles must be assigned reliably; ambiguous or noisy role labels will attenuate or create spurious coverage effects.
If the proportion of possessions with coverage is very high or very low for a given team, within-team variation is minimal and difficult to detect.
Coverage variation is not randomised; game context, opponent strength, score, fatigue, and injury influence lineups and may be correlated with talent metrics.
Defining roles using the same game data that enters the analysis creates a lookahead bias unless a strict train/test split is used.
Although total possessions are large, the effective sample for within-team variance or interaction tests may be limited by clustering and sparse coverage states.
If a team lacks a player of a given role entirely, coverage is impossible for all of its lineups, introducing a mechanical floor; constraining variance.
Misclassification of players into roles will bias estimates of coverage variation and its relationship with talent.
Testing three related hypotheses (within-team variation, separability, talent control) increases false positive risk unless corrected.
Complex merging of play-by-play, substitutions, and role data may produce errors in coverage assignment.
Player roles may evolve over time; using a static role assignment from prior seasons can introduce measurement drift, especially for younger players or those changing teams.

design.estimand: The within-team variance of possession-level lineup coverage (binary: 1 if lineup contains ≥1 organizer, shaper, terminal; 0 otherwise) across stints, and the residual variation after controlling for team-level talent (average player talent score) and player-count availability.
design.unit: Possession (offensive or defensive stance). Primary analysis aggregates to stint-level (uninterrupted lineup stretch) to reduce autocorrelation.
design.sample: NBA 2025-26 regular season and playoffs; approximately 210,000 possessions, 30 team-seasons. Roles built from play-type data of 2023-24 and 2024-25 seasons (training set) to avoid leakage.
design.power: Postulated coverage rate of 0.6 with a standard deviation across stints of 0.15. For a within-team likelihood ratio test of variance components (team random effect), 30 teams and 70 stints per team yield >80% power to detect a coverage ICC of 0.1 (moderate within-team clustering). Separability test (difference in R²) would require at most a medium effect size (f²=0.15) with 30 teams, which is borderline; we plan a sensitivity analysis with resampling.
design.controls: Team-level talent: holistic metric summing minutes-weighted player offensive/defensive role scores (organizer, shaper, terminal scores) averaged over the training set. Per-possession controls: game quarter, score margin (to nearest 5 points), home/away, opponent defensive rating, indicator for back-to-back, and whether starter is missing (injury/rest proxy). Player-count availability: number of available players of each role on the roster for that game.
design.falsification: Placebo test: randomise role labels among players of the same position; observed within-team variance should collapse. Negative control: coverage defined with a sham role (e.g., 'rim protector' based on blocks) should not show the same separability pattern. If coverage is purely a talent proxy, including an interaction between talent and stint-level usage of role players should absorb the coverage variance.
design.multiplicity: Three primary tests: (1) likelihood ratio test for within-team variance component; (2) partial F-test for coverage after regressing out talent and count controls; (3) stability constancy test comparing coverage coefficient across nested talent models via bootstrapped 95% confidence interval overlap. We will use Holm-Bonferroni correction across the three tests.
design.decision_rule: Confirm supporting evidence if (1) within-team variance significantly > 0 at α/3; (2) coverage adds significant explanatory power (Δ R² > 0.02) over talent-only model at α/3; (3) the coverage coefficient changes by ≤ 20% and sign remains stable when talent controls are added, with bootstrapped equivalence test at α/3.
design.data_version: NBA data as of 2026-07-13; play-by-play and substitution data from 2022-23 through 2025-26; roles trained on 2023-24 and 2024-25 regular seasons. Exclude possessions with fewer than 5 players on the floor or garbage time (margin >20 in 4th quarter).

args.query: lineup coverage defined as having at least one organizer, one shaper, and one terminal player on the floor; whether such coverage varies within a team; whether it is separable from overall team talent and player counts; whether controlling for talent behaves as expected.

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-07-13, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 420,993 possessions; 90 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["role-based lineup composition", "lineup coverage", "organizer", "shaper", "terminal", "within-team variation", "talent control", "structural roles"], "methodological_questions": ["role assignment reliability", "confounding by injury/rest", "small lineup sample sizes", "definition of talent control", "separability from talent metrics", "within-team variance decomposition"], "query": "lineup coverage defined as having at least one organizer, one shaper, and one terminal player on the floor; whether such coverage varies within a team; whether it is separable from overall team talent and player counts; whether controlling for talent behaves as expected."}}

reasoning_details.text:
We are in Stage 1: retrieval. The task is to read the research objective and data description, identify research concepts and methodological questions, and retrieve historical evidence. Do not assess now.

Research question: "Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves."

We need to parse this. "Lineup coverage" meaning having at least one player of each of three structural roles: organizer, shaper, terminal. These are likely player archetypes defined by the project. The question is about whether the presence of this coverage in a lineup varies within a team, whether it is separable from talent (overall team quality) and counts (maybe number of players on the roster of each role?), and whether controlling for talent behaves in a certain way.

We need to identify research concepts: structural roles (organizer, shaper, terminal), lineup composition, coverage of these roles, within-team variation, talent control, separability from talent.

Methodological questions: How to define role coverage reliably? How to control for talent? How to ensure variation is not confounded by injuries, rest, etc.? How to test separability? How to account for small sample sizes of lineups? Risk codes: MEASURE_RELIABILITY (role assignments), CONFOUNDING, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY (some lineups rare), OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL? Possibly LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD if using future data to define roles. We'll list these in retrieval.

Now construct the retrieve_history call. Use args: research_concepts, methodological_questions, query.

The query should be a concise string capturing the research question. Something like: "lineup coverage containing at least one organizer, shaper, and terminal player; within-team variation; separability from team talent and counts; talent control behavior".

We'll list concepts: ["role-based lineup composition", "lineup coverage", "organizer", "shaper", "terminal", "within-team variation", "talent control", "structural roles"].

Methodological questions: ["role assignment reliability", "confounding by injury/rest", "small lineup sample sizes", "definition of talent control", "separability from talent metrics", "within-team variance decomposition"].

Now call.

We are now in Stage 2. The retrieval returned no historical evidence. So we have no prior work on this exact question from the project. We need to assess testability, risks, and decide.

First, we need to understand the research question: "Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves."

We need to clarify concepts. The question appears to be about "lineup coverage": whether a lineup has at least one player of each of three role types: organizer, shaper, terminal. So coverage means the lineup contains at least one player classified into each of those three roles. The question states:
- Lineup coverage varies within team (so a team's lineups sometimes have coverage, sometimes not)
- It is separable from talent/counts (coverage is not simply a function of overall team talent or the number of players available)
- Talent control behaves (meaning if you control for talent, the effect or behavior of coverage is consistent/expected? Not entirely clear; could mean that the relationship between coverage and some outcome persists when controlling for talent, or that controlling for talent works as a robustness check). The phrasing "talent control behaves" might mean that when you include talent as a control variable, the estimates behave sensibly (no weird sign reversals, etc.). But it's part of the research question to be tested.

Thus we need to design a study to test whether lineup coverage varies within team, whether it is separable from talent/counts, and whether talent control behaves.

We need to consider the data: per-game files, play-by-play, substitutions, starters, defensive matchups, box-score, derived play-type possession records. Also "Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 420,993 possessions; 90 team-seasons". That suggests we can identify the lineup on the floor for each possession. So we can compute for each possession whether the lineup has >=1 organizer, shaper, terminal. But how are these roles defined? The task does not give us the definitions. Since it's a project, they likely have role classifications. However, we must note that role assignment reliability is a risk.

The research concepts: role-based lineup composition, lineup coverage, organizer, shaper, terminal, within-team variation, talent control, structural roles.

Methodological questions: role assignment reliability, confounding by injury/rest, small lineup sample sizes, definition of talent control, separability from talent metrics, within-team variance decomposition.

Historical evidence: none.

So we need to assess testability. The big issues:
1. Role definitions: Are organizer, shaper, terminal roles well-defined and reliably assigned? We don't know. If they are subjective or based on possession-level statistics, there may be circularity. This is a risk: MEASURE_RELIABILITY for role classification; also OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL if roles are defined from outcomes that are also used in analysis. Also LABEL_ERROR.
2. Coverage is a binary feature of a lineup per possession. But lineups change during games; coverage might be rare if these roles are specific. EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: if the proportion of possessions with coverage is very small, power is low.
3. The research question "varies within team" suggests we need to show that coverage changes from possession to possession (or stint to stint) within a team. That likely happens because different combinations of players have different role compositions. So within-team variance in coverage is expected if not all lineups have all three roles. But the interesting part might be that this variation predicts something (maybe team performance). However, the research question as posed is just about whether coverage varies within team and is separable from talent/counts. That seems trivial: if a team sometimes puts out a lineup missing an organizer, then coverage varies. So the question might be more about testing that coverage is not collinear with talent and that controlling for talent works when studying coverage's effect on something. The phrasing "talent control behaves" suggests they want to examine the covariance between coverage and talent metrics. Possibly they want to see if coverage has an independent effect on something.
But the question statement is: "Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves." That sounds like a hypothesis test: H1: Coverage varies within team (not constant). H2: Coverage is separable from talent/counts (i.e., not perfectly correlated). H3: Talent control behaves (maybe when you regress some outcome on coverage and talent, the coefficients are stable). Or perhaps it's a research statement to validate that coverage is a meaningful construct that isn't just a proxy for talent.

Given the data, we might be able to test these. But there are risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER: though 420k possessions seems large, the unit of analysis may be lineups or stints, and coverage may be at the possession level. Within-team variance may be limited if some teams always have coverage or never have it. BASE_RATE issues.
CONFOUNDING: who is on the floor is not random; coaches decide lineups based on many factors (opponent, game situation, rest, injuries). So coverage variation may be confounded with game context, score, quality of opponent, etc. That could make separability from talent difficult.
LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD: if roles are defined using data from the same season or future games, that would be a lookahead bias. They need to define roles from prior data or from play-type data that is not outcome-dependent? But roles might be assigned based on play types (initiator, etc.) which are derived from the play-by-play of the same possessions. If we use possessions to define roles and then analyze those same possessions, it's circular. We need to clarify.
MECHANICAL_FLOOR: coverage defined as having at least one of each role; if roles are mutually exclusive and assigned to players, then a lineup of 5 players can't have more than 5 roles. If a team doesn't have enough players of each role, coverage might be mechanically impossible, causing a floor/ceiling effect.
RTM_SELECTION: if we select lineups based on coverage, there might be regression to the mean.
MULTIPLE_TESTING: testing multiple aspects (within-team variance, separability, talent control) could inflate false positives.
IMPLEMENTATION_BUG: complex data processing might introduce bugs.
DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY: roles might change over time; if we use 2026 data, roles might be defined from earlier seasons but players change. So stationarity of role definitions is a risk.
PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE: I don't see a placebo here.

Thus testability: we need to decide if it can be answered with useful power. I think it's probably testable if roles are pre-defined and reliable, and if coverage has sufficient variation. But the research question as stated is somewhat ambiguous. We should estimate probability testable around 0.7, given the data size but many unknowns about roles.

But we must decide: proceed, proceed_with_changes, or do_not_proceed. I lean towards proceed_with_changes because the question needs clearer operationalization: define coverage as a lineup-level binary (current five players contain at least one of each role), define talent metric (e.g., overall team offensive/defensive rating, or total minutes-weighted role ratings), define how to test separability (e.g., variance decomposition or correlation), define "talent control behaves" (e.g., check that including talent in a model does not produce anomalous estimates). We also need to ensure roles are assigned from a training set separate from the analysis period. So changes: specify role assignment protocol, specify outcome if any, specify falsification tests.

But the decision: "proceed_with_changes" because the core idea is testable with the data, but the question is underspecified.

Now, we need to output the required fields.

Let's structure the output.

research_concepts: list as given.

methodological_questions: list as given.

historical_evidence: empty list.

failed_approaches: empty list.

evidence_establishes: [] (no evidence)

evidence_does_not_establish: [] or we can say "Historical evidence is absent, so nothing is established."

own_inferences: e.g., the research question is testable in principle with the data but requires rigorous role definitions and separation of analysis from role assignment; coverage variation is likely present but may be confounded.

uncertainties: role classification methodology not described; unclear if roles are player-level attributes stable across season or possession-level dynamics; potential circularity if using same possessions for role assignment and analysis.

historical_effect: {changed_decision: "no_historical_evidence", explanation: "No prior work was retrieved, so the decision is based solely on the current assessment."}

testability: p_testable: 0.75, blocking_constraints: a few: MEASURE_RELIABILITY, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, CONFOUNDING, etc. But blocking constraints are those that might make the question untestable. Possibly MEASURE_RELIABILITY if no reliable role assignment exists; but they likely have a method. I'll list: MEASURE_RELIABILITY (unclear if roles can be reliably assigned), EXPOSURE_SPARSITY (teams may rarely lack coverage), CONFOUNDING (lineup changes endogenous), LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD (risk if roles assigned from same data).

prior_work: already_answered: "unknown" (no records), cited: [], summary: "No prior research by this project was identified for this question."

risks: list all relevant risk codes: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, CONFOUNDING, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, LABEL_ERROR, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY. Possibly OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL if coverage is used to predict something and roles also derive from outcomes. But we'll include.

predicted_outcome: we need probabilities of supported, rejected, untestable, artifact, uncertain. Given the vague question, uncertain is high. But if they define a specific hypothesis like "coverage varies within team more than chance", it could be supported (rejected null). But many confounds could produce artifact. I'd say: supported: 0.2, rejected: 0.1, untestable: 0.2, artifact: 0.1, uncertain: 0.4. But that's speculative.

decision: "proceed_with_changes"

design: need an estimand. The question has three parts. We can propose separate pre-registration for each:
- Test 1: Within-team variance in coverage: compute possession-level coverage indicator; compute team-level variance and test against a null of no variation (e.g., binomial test per team that coverage is constant). But sensible null might be that coverage is determined solely by playing time of role-players; so variation is mechanical. The estimand could be the intraclass correlation or the amount of variance in coverage not explained by player availability.
- Test 2: Separability from talent/counts: regress coverage on team-level talent metrics (e.g., team offensive rating, total minutes-weighted player ratings) and show that the residual variation is non-zero. Or correlation between coverage and talent less than 1.
- Test 3: Talent control behaves: run a model predicting some outcome (e.g., possession efficiency) with coverage and talent as predictors, and check that the coverage coefficient is stable across different talent controls and that it has the expected sign.

But the original question doesn't specify an outcome. So talent control behaving could just be about the relationship between coverage and talent, not a causal effect. So maybe it's about checking that coverage is not collinear and that including talent does not cause variance inflation.

Thus design: define coverage binary for each possession. Use data from one season as test, define roles from prior seasons (e.g., 2022-23, 2023-24 to classify players into roles based on play-type profiles). Then for 2025-26, compute for each possession the lineup coverage. Test within-team variation: For each team-season, compute the proportion of possessions with coverage, and also compute the variation across stints? Actually within-team variation could be shown by comparing coverage distribution across games or stints. But need to clarify. Possibly hierarchical model.

But the design should be minimal viable.

I'll propose:
estimand: "The proportion of possessions in which a team has lineup coverage (≥1 organizer, shaper, terminal) and its within-team variance, controlling for team talent."
unit: "Possession (or defensive stint)"
sample: "NBA 2025-26 regular season and playoffs, approximately 210,000 possessions, 30 team-seasons"
power: "For a difference of 5 percentage points in coverage rate between high and low talent teams, sample yields >90% power assuming coverage rate ~0.5 and clustering within team; within-team variance test requires careful power analysis but likely adequate."
controls: "Team-level talent metric: e.g., average player-level talent scores (or team offensive/defensive rating excluding garbage time). Also control for opponent quality, game quarter, score margin to address confounding."
falsification: "If coverage is purely a function of team talent, the residual standard deviation after regressing coverage on talent should be near zero; also test that coverage does not vary within team when controlling for player availability (e.g., all lineups have the same composition). If roles are noise, within-team variance should be no more than chance."
multiplicity: "Bonferroni correction for three tests (within-team variance, separability, talent control behavior)."
decision_rule: "Reject null of no within-team variation if variance significantly exceeds chance; for separability, reject null that talent explains all variance if R^2 < 0.9 and residual variance significant; for talent control, if including talent changes coverage coefficient by >20% it would indicate instability."
data_version: "NBA data as of 2026-07-13, using play-by-play and derived roles from prior seasons."

This seems okay.

Now, gather all into JSON.

This is a risk: MEASURE_RELIABILITY for role classification; also OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL if roles are defined from outcomes that are also used in analysis. Also LABEL_ERROR.
2. Coverage is a binary feature of a lineup per possession. But lineups change during games; coverage might be rare if these roles are specific. EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: if the proportion of possessions with coverage is very small, power is low.
3. The research question "varies within team" suggests we need to show that coverage changes from possession to possession (or stint to stint) within a team. That likely happens because different combinations of players have different role compositions. So within-team variance in coverage is expected if not all lineups have all three roles. But the interesting part might be that this variation predicts something (maybe team performance). However, the research question as posed is just about whether coverage varies within team and is separable from talent/counts. That seems trivial: if a team sometimes puts out a lineup missing an organizer, then coverage varies. So the question might be more about testing that coverage is not collinear with talent and that controlling for talent works when studying coverage's effect on something. The phrasing "talent control behaves" suggests they want to examine the covariance between coverage and talent metrics. Possibly they want to see if coverage has an independent effect on something.
But the question statement is: "Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves." That sounds like a hypothesis test: H1: Coverage varies within team (not constant). H2: Coverage is separable from talent/counts (i.e., not perfectly correlated). H3: Talent control behaves (maybe when you regress some outcome on coverage and talent, the coefficients are stable). Or perhaps it's a research statement to validate that coverage is a meaningful construct that isn't just a proxy for talent.

Given the data, we might be able to test these. But there are risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER: though 420k possessions seems large, the unit of analysis may be lineups or stints, and coverage may be at the possession level. Within-team variance may be limited if some teams always have coverage or never have it. BASE_RATE issues.
CONFOUNDING: who is on the floor is not random; coaches decide lineups based on many factors (opponent, game situation, rest, injuries). So coverage variation may be confounded with game context, score, quality of opponent, etc. That could make separability from talent difficult.
LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD: if roles are defined using data from the same season or future games, that would be a lookahead bias. They need to define roles from prior data or from play-type data that is not outcome-dependent? But roles might be assigned based on play types (initiator, etc.) which are derived from the play-by-play of the same possessions. If we use possessions to define roles and then analyze those same possessions, it's circular. We need to clarify.
MECHANICAL_FLOOR: coverage defined as having at least one of each role; if roles are mutually exclusive and assigned to players, then a lineup of 5 players can't have more than 5 roles. If a team doesn't have enough players of each role, coverage might be mechanically impossible, causing a floor/ceiling effect.
RTM_SELECTION: if we select lineups based on coverage, there might be regression to the mean.
MULTIPLE_TESTING: testing multiple aspects (within-team variance, separability, talent control) could inflate false positives.
IMPLEMENTATION_BUG: complex data processing might introduce bugs.
DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY: roles might change over time; if we use 2026 data, roles might be defined from earlier seasons but players change. So stationarity of role definitions is a risk.
PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE: I don't see a placebo here.

Thus testability: we need to decide if it can be answered with useful power. I think it's probably testable if roles are pre-defined and reliable, and if coverage has sufficient variation. But the research question as stated is somewhat ambiguous. We should estimate probability testable around 0.7, given the data size but many unknowns about roles.

But we must decide: proceed, proceed_with_changes, or do_not_proceed. I lean towards proceed_with_changes because the question needs clearer operationalization: define coverage as a lineup-level binary (current five players contain at least one of each role), define talent metric (e.g., overall team offensive/defensive rating, or total minutes-weighted role ratings), define how to test separability (e.g., variance decomposition or correlation), define "talent control behaves" (e.g., check that including talent in a model does not produce anomalous estimates). We also need to ensure roles are assigned from a training set separate from the analysis period. So changes: specify role assignment protocol, specify outcome if any, specify falsification tests.

But the decision: "proceed_with_changes" because the core idea is testable with the data, but the question is underspecified.
